title: GothamChess European Tour Kicks Off On October 25 With Special Guests And Activities
summary: Europe is about to meet the world's biggest chess creator in person again. IM Levy Rozman, better known as GothamChess, is returning to the old continent for his second tour from October 25 to November 10. Fans in six cities can get tickets to see Levy up close—and enjoy the many attractions and guests lined up for the tour.

title: President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev receives FIDE President Timur Turlov
summary: President of the Republic of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev received newly elected FIDE President Timur Turlov and congratulated him on his election to lead the International Chess Federation. During the meeting, the sides discussed the development of chess in Kazakhstan, the country’s growing role in the international chess community, and further cooperation between FIDE and the Kazakhstan Chess Federation. President Tokayev noted that chess holds a special place in Kazakhstan, serving not only as a sport but also as a vital tool for developing the intellectual potential of the younger generation. He also highlighted the recent progress of Kazakh chess school, including the strong results of its national teams and the silver medal won by the Kazakhstan’s women’s team at the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Currently, more than 278,000 people across Kazakhstan are actively engaged in chess, reflecting the rapid growth of the game in the country in recent years. President Tokayev stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation between the Kazakhstan Chess Federation and FIDE. This includes advancing educational initiatives, providing professional development for coaches and arbiters, and hosting major international chess events in Kazakhstan. FIDE President Timur Turlov, who also serves as President of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, noted that the country’s experience could serve as a valuable example of how government support, coordinated investment, educational integration, and federation development can produce measurable results. He observed that over the past three years, Kazakhstan has achieved significant progress, marked by strong results from top players and national teams, the wider introduction of chess in schools, greater investment in coach training, and expanded opportunities for young players across the country.  Turlov added that Kazakhstan’s experience demonstrates how a systematic approach and close cooperation among the federation, government, schools, and the private sector can accelerate the growth of chess. As FIDE President, he intends to help other national federations develop stronger systems adapted to their unique circumstances while sharing Kazakhstan’s effective practices with the global chess community. President Turlov also briefed President Tokayev on FIDE’s priorities for the coming years, which include expanding chess in education, strengthening support for national federations, improving professional training for coaches and arbiters, developing youth chess, and creating more opportunities for international cooperation.  The meeting concluded with President Tokayev wishing President Turlov every success in his new role as FIDE President.

title: The 2026/27 season of the Bundesliga kicks off this weekend
summary:
Three matches per weekend

The new Chess Bundesliga season begins on Friday at 4 p.m. The teams will not have much time to settle in, however. Three rounds are scheduled within just three days - a consequence of the new calendar, which reduces the previous seven Bundesliga weekends to five dates, each featuring three match days. The season begins on 9 October and ends from 2 to 4 April 2027 with the central final round in Neuwied.

The convincing champions of the 2026/27 season: SC Viernheim | Photo: Nils Rohde

From a sporting perspective, the picture remains familiar: SC Viernheim enter the season as defending champions, while OSG Baden-Baden are once again the strongest team on paper. With an average Elo of 2718.5, according to our statistics , Baden-Baden are ahead of Viernheim, who come in at 2692.6. The gap alone, however, says little about how the season will unfold. Last year already showed that it is not only nominal strength that matters, but above all which players are actually sitting at the boards. This is precisely where Baden-Baden will be hoping for greater consistency this time.

Comprehensive live commentary at last

In recent years, there have rightly been calls for live commentary befitting one of the "strongest leagues in the world". That is exactly what will be introduced for the season beginning on Friday. SC Viernheim have already regularly offered live commentary with GM Ilja Zaragatski and Angelika Valkova, although this focused mainly on their own club. That coverage will continue. Other clubs, such as St. Pauli and Bayern Munich, have also occasionally provided similar accompanying coverage. FC Bayern will again offer commentary on the games from Munich this coming weekend, with GM Klaus Bischoff at the microphone (MSA Zugzwang are the hosts).

The most comprehensive and significant new offering, however, comes from the German Chess Federation: Schachdeutschlandtv will provide extensive coverage of the full match days on YouTube and Twitch. WGM Josefine Safarli and WCM Katharina Reinecke will launch the coverage this weekend.

Team Top four players

1. SC Viernheim Abdusattorov, Duda, Van Foreest, Mamedyarov

2. OSG Baden-Baden Caruana, Sindarov, Keymer, Anand

3. SK Kirchweyhe Saric, Predke, Ter-Sahakyan, Brkic

4. FC Bayern München Fedoseev, Yakubboev, Alekseenko, Santos

5. Hamburger SK F. Svane, R. Svane, Mendonca, Banusz

6. SV Werder Bremen Martirosyan, Ivic, McShane, Gumularz

7. SG Solingen Harikrishna, Navara, L'Ami, Ragger

8. Düsseldorfer SK Murzin, Bologan, Ghazarian, Kobalia

9. SC Heimbach-Weis-Neuwied Sargsyan, Hakobyan, Lodici, Finek

10. FC St. Pauli Carlsen, Rapport, Pranav, Theodorou

11. SF Bad Mergentheim Rodshtein, Kazakovskiy, Pultenivicius, Laurusas

12. SV Deggendorf Erigaisi, Indjic, Narayanan, Ghosh

13. MSA Zugzwang Eljanov, Hovhannisyan, Costa, Horvath

14. SF Berlin Movsesian, Moranda, Tomczak, Neiksans

15. SC Remagen Sinzig Ivanchuk, Gledura, Volokitin, Pavlidis

16. SV Erkenschwick 1923 Kantans, Meshkovs, Vrolijk, De Winter

Viernheim enter the fray as defending champions

The champions open against promoted side SV Erkenschwick 1923, whom Viernheim recently defeated in the cup final. On paper, the roles are clearly defined. Viernheim have an exceptionally strong lineup and have largely kept their leading players in the roster. Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Jan-Krzysztof Duda, Jorden van Foreest and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov head a team aiming to defend their title. Aydin Suleymanli has been added to the squad.

Parham Maghsoodloo (left) played throughout last season on board three and scored a strong 4½/7 - pictured here against Ihor Samunenkov, whose club Wolfhagen withdrew after finishing third in their debut season | Photo: Stefan Liebig¿

After the opening match against Erkenschwick, another task awaits on Saturday: SC Heimbach-Weis-Neuwied. On Sunday, Viernheim face Werder Bremen. The 12-year-old Argentine prodigy Faustino Oro is the second-youngest grandmaster in chess history and, if he plays, will attract additional attention in Bremen.

Baden-Baden hopefully field their stars

Baden-Baden also begin against a traditional club, facing SG Solingen on Friday. A day later they meet newly promoted SC Remagen Sinzig, before completing the weekend on Sunday against SV Deggendorf.

Bundesliga fans would be delighted to see many games featuring this pair: Viswanathan Anand and Vincent Keymer | Photo: Stefan Liebig

Baden-Baden have made targeted changes to their squad compared with last season. Anish Giri, Alireza Firouzja and Levon Aronian are no longer in the lineup. In their place, among others, German stars Matthias Bluebaum and Dimitrij Kollars have joined the team, as well as Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Maxime Lagarde. Fabiano Caruana, Javokhir Sindarov, Vincent Keymer, Viswanathan Anand and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave remain in the squad. The decisive question, however, will be how regularly these players can actually be fielded.

St. Pauli and Bayern in the chasing pack

The opening weekend is particularly interesting with regard to the battles featuring FC Bayern Munich, Hamburger SK, FC St. Pauli and MSA Zugzwang. Bayern face Hamburger SK on Friday, followed by MSA Zugzwang on Saturday and St. Pauli on Sunday. Hamburger SK, meanwhile, play St. Pauli on Saturday and Zugzwang on Sunday.

St. Pauli once again enter the season with a prominent name: Magnus Carlsen leads the squad, with another world-class player, Richard Rapport, behind him. Whether Carlsen will actually be available remains uncertain, as in previous years. Even so, the club have significantly improved their average Elo and are nominally part of the chasing group behind Baden-Baden and Viernheim.

Bayern have also strengthened their squad. Nodirbek Yakubboev joins the team and is expected to play on board two behind Vladimir Fedoseev. This puts Munich among the teams aiming to establish themselves in the fight for the leading places.

Promoted teams face different test

While the teams at the top are already talking about championship points, the promoted sides face a different kind of early test. Alongside Erkenschwick, Bad Mergentheim and Remagen Sinzig are new or returning to the Bundesliga. Vasyl Ivanchuk is listed on board one for Remagen Sinzig. The living and still very active chess legend has been associated with the club for many years.

Bad Mergentheim begin against Düsseldorfer SK, play SF Berlin on Saturday and face Kirchweyhe on Sunday. Remagen Sinzig first meet Deggendorf, then Baden-Baden and finally Solingen. The promoted squad therefore faces an extremely difficult assignment as early as the second match day.

Erkenschwick likewise have little chance to catch their breath after opening against Viernheim: they face Werder Bremen on Saturday before meeting Heimbach-Weis-Neuwied on Sunday.

Three days, nine matches per playing group

The new schedule also changes the rhythm of the season. The opening three rounds form a compact block in which early gaps in the table could develop quickly. At the same time, no long-term conclusions should be drawn from a single defeat. Once again this season, the league is characterised by a clear gap between the two leading teams, a strong chasing group and a broad midfield.

The new format is intended above all to make scheduling easier and improve the availability of top players. Five weekends instead of seven reduce travel and organisational demands and are intended to limit clashes with international tournaments. The basic principle remains unchanged: 16 teams compete over 8 boards for match points, with the final totals deciding the championship and relegation.

title: Frederik Svane: An understated Olympic record
summary:
Before Svane, only one German player had ever won two gold medals at an Olympiad: Dr Robert Hübner. In 1972 in Skopje, he scored 15 points from 18 games, or 83.3 percent, to win gold on board one. Eighteen years later, in 1990 in Novi Sad, he won gold again. Hübner scored 7 points from 10 games on board one and therefore finished "only" fifth in the board-one standings, but with a performance rating of 2734 he achieved the best result of all Olympiad participants and received his second gold medal for it.

Robert Hübner in 1971 | Photo: Bert Verhoeff, Anefo

In fact, the rules for awarding medals for the best individual performances at Chess Olympiads have changed several times over the course of history. At the first official Olympiad in London in 1927, there was no fixed board order. The best individual results in the tournament as a whole were rewarded. A similar system was used in 1928, but in Hamburg in 1930 the absolute number of points scored was what counted. That is why Akiba Rubinstein, Poland's board one, won gold with 15/17. Had the medals been awarded according to percentage score, Alexander Alekhine, who played on board one for France, would have won gold with 9/9.

From 1931 onwards, however, the percentage score was decisive, although special rules were introduced from time to time over the decades. From 1984 through to 2006, not only were gold, silver and bronze medals awarded for the best percentage scores on the individual boards, but three additional medals were also awarded for the best tournament performance ratings in the tournament as a whole. This meant that a player could win three medals at a single Olympiad: one with the team, one for one of the three best results on his board and one for his performance rating.

John Nunn achieved this feat at the 1984 Olympiad in Thessaloniki. With England, he won silver in the team competition, scored 10 points from 11 games to win gold on board two, and also won gold for the best performance rating of the entire tournament with a TPR of 2868.

John Nunn in 1982 | Photo: Rob Croes, Anefo

In 2008, however, the additional performance classification was abolished again, and since then the best performance rating on each individual board has counted.

According to the OlimpBase database , neither Frederik Svane nor Dr Robert Hübner holds the German record for the most board prizes. That distinction belongs to Karl-May-Magazin publisher and arbiter Lothar Schmid, who won silver on board two four times: in Dubrovnik in 1950, Helsinki in 1952, Lugano in 1968 and Siegen in 1970. This comparison includes all players who represented Germany from the first official Chess Olympiad in 1927 onwards: during the Weimar Republic, the Nazi era, for West Germany and East Germany, and for reunified Germany.

Lothar Schmid at the 1960 Chess Olympiad in Leipzig | Photo: Tournament book

But Schmid's record could also be broken sooner or later by Frederik Svane, who is only 22. The next Chess Olympiad will take place in Abu Dhabi in 2028.

title: From Dusk till Dawn
summary:
Against digital isolation

In earlier times, chess culture was widespread in many countries. People sat together in cafés, talked about the affairs of the world and played chess at the same time. Some academic careers, admittedly, came to an early end because of constant visits to chess cafés, and the Nobel Prizes later went to others. If the chess cafés happened to be closed, or if the players had been thrown out because they were always too loud and ordered too little, they simply met in private instead, preferably in groups.

Of course, they played blitz. In a group, they could organise small tournaments or make sarcastic comments from the sidelines about the moves being played. As everyone knows, you can always see more from the outside. The longer the evening went on, the more unpredictable and exciting the games became. The steady consumption of stimulating drinks increased the fun factor - but also the element of chance. There was no tournament silence, but there was Slade or some other loud musical racket instead. People could spend decades retelling the stories of their brilliant combinations. Lifelong friendships were formed.

"Enjoy your time, for you only live in the here and now. Tomorrow you cannot make up for yesterday, and later comes sooner than you think."

And then the internet was invented. Now you can play blitz anytime and anywhere. And against anyone in the world. That is, of course, a wonderful thing. You no longer have to go to a chess café to play blitz, nor to a blitz tournament at the club... Chess, however, became a rather anonymous affair. You do not see your online opponent, you do not know where they live, you do not know their name. The usernames are anonymous. You cannot talk about the game either. No time, next game. All the games are recorded digitally. But who needs that? Where is the chess culture?

A seasoned chess aficionado from Hamburg - who prefers not to be named - has now come up with a fine idea. In memory of the good old days, he organised a private chess tournament, just like in the past.

He invited all the chess friends with whom he had met for sociable blitz chess since his youth along his journey through life in northern Germany. In Hamburg-Stellingen, he found a suitable venue for the event. The formerly young players gladly accepted the invitation. Almost 40 chess enthusiasts came together, including even a few who had never known life without the internet and mobile phones.

As the event was private, the pictures here could only be taken with a hidden camera - but at least they could be taken. The tension in the games is palpable.

The tournament was held under the motto "The 12 Hours of Stellingen" - in other words, a blitz chess marathon, "From Dusk till Dawn", so to speak. It began in the early afternoon, in classic fashion: with preliminary rounds and a sliding-board system. The player at the head of the table records the result and turns the board around.

It was not entirely retro, however. Modern digital chess clocks made a time control of 3+2 possible. That did not exist in the old days, only analogue clocks, which were sometimes given quite a pounding in blitz because the buttons on top used to stick.

There was music again too. Slade also got an airing. The private tournament was better organised than many an official event. There were breaks in between, cake and later soup. Coffee pots were available to help maintain alertness, at least at the beginning. After nightfall, the participants moved on to more cheerful drinks.

The official tournament had already finished at around eleven o'clock, but the intended marathon time target had not yet been reached. For the prize winners, the mysterious organiser had put together some worthy prizes from his own collection. Full of anticipation, he had personally painted the winner's trophy with real gold paint.

Tournament preparations

After the official tournament ended, the chess friends switched to casual blitz. By around one o'clock, only the hard core remained, though that still amounted to a quarter of the original field. Then someone suggested that the remaining players should play a proper blitz tournament. And so they did.

A highly recommended activity for others to try!
